key_insight: STEM replaces the FFN up-projection with a static, token-indexed embedding lookup while keeping the gate and down-projection dense, removing runtime routing and enabling asynchronous CPU offload. This decouples parameter capacity from per-token compute and communication overhead.
problem_solved: Addresses instability, load-balancing and communication overheads of fine‑grained sparse modules (e.g., MoE-style up-projections) by eliminating runtime routing and per-token remote fetches.
method: Replace FFN up-projection with a layer-local, token-indexed embedding module (static lookup)
Keep gating and FFN down-projection dense to preserve expressivity and stable gradients
Enable CPU offload of large embedding tables with asynchronous prefetch to remove runtime routing/communication hotspots
impact: Provides a practical way to scale transformer capacity without proportional per‑token compute or costly routing, simplifying training and deployment while reducing memory/communication pressure.
visual_elements: Annotated transformer block diagram showing: token → embedding lookup (replacing up-projection) → dense gate → dense down-projection
Bar chart comparing parameters vs per-token compute for dense FFN, MoE, and STEM
Timeline/flow illustration contrasting runtime routing (MoE) vs asynchronous prefetch (STEM) highlighting lower latency and no load-balancing step
Heatmap or icon set showing benefits: training stability, lower communication, CPU offload, and higher capacity
paper_title: STEM: Scaling Transformers with Embedding Modules
paper_authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan, Sheng Cao, Harry Dong, Changsheng Zhao, Attiano Purpura-Pontoniere
